content.title: Trapped in Dystopia: Violence Increases Over a Month After the Ceuta Influx
content.lead: Suffering in Spain's North African exclave: Refugees and residents affected as opposition plans protests on city holiday.
content.author: Florian Haupt, Barcelona

image.author: Marcos Moreno / Getty
image.caption: Playa del Trampolín in Ceuta is a hotspot: Migrants gather here, unsure where else to go, hoping for food distributions. Police have cleared the area several times, but people keep returning. Last week, there were attacks, presumably by right-wing extremists.
image.altText: CEUTA, SPAIN - AUGUST 31: Dozens of migrants are walking along Trampoline beach on August 31, 2026 in Ceuta, Spain. Trampoline beach is once again home to a large number of makeshift shacks, despite migrants having previously been moved to other designated areas. The site, which is also used by the Red Cross to distribute food, had been considered to have been cleared as a settlement. (Photo By Marcos Moreno/Europa Press via Getty Images)

content.caption: Playa del Trampolín in Ceuta is a hotspot: Migrants gather here, unsure where else to go, hoping for food distributions. Police have cleared the area several times, but people keep returning. Last week, there were attacks, presumably by right-wing extremists.
content.author: Marcos Moreno / Getty

content.text: Monday was the day of return. Few countries maintain a collective holiday period as steadfastly as Spain, where almost the entire country shuts down in August. Political activity was no exception; on Monday, that too returned. On television, many popular morning shows broadcast live from Ceuta as a central point of discussion.

Even more than a month after thousands of refugees entered the exclave and at least 150 migrants died, Ceuta dominates all debates in the kingdom. It was a place last visited by a Spanish king 19 years ago; a place that always had a rather exotic character; a place most Spaniards knew only from textbooks and found harder to reach than London, Zurich, or Istanbul. Since July 30, it seems to have become something like the country's soul and conscience.

Images of frustration and anger, of helplessness and exhaustion, wash across the sea to the mainland. Refugees and residents appear trapped in the same dystopia. Some live in miserable conditions, wander the streets, and still do not know where to go a month later. Others lament the loss of normality and are becoming increasingly violent. Last week, a tent camp was set on fire and Red Cross food distributions were blocked. Police and military, it seems, must protect everyone and everything from all quarters.

In some bakeries, bread is rationed. Sexual offenses have increased, and underage refugee girls are reportedly forced into prostitution in exchange for a single dinner. Parents fear for their children. Muslims often no longer feel like neighbors but rather like suspects. Regardless of religion, those who could left the city in August and traveled to family members or second homes on the mainland.

This Wednesday is now «Día de Ceuta.» The city holiday commemorates the year 1415, when João I of Portugal appointed Count Pedro de Menezes as governor on September 2, formally integrating Ceuta into his kingdom. In the 17th century, sovereignty passed to Spain, and there, the Federation of Municipalities and Provinces (FEMP) called for national solidarity rallies for Ceuta in all cities on Wednesday.

image.author: Marcos Moreno / Imago
image.caption: The national flag is the symbol of protests against the refugees, who sometimes need police protection. For the people of Ceuta, the exclave's belonging to Spain is beyond question.
image.altText: Protest Against Migrants in Ceuta: Several people during a demonstration to protest the situation caused by the mass arrival of migrants, on August 27, 2026, in Ceuta, Spain. content.text: The FEMP is controlled by the conservative party, which also wants the demonstrations to be understood as a vote against the socialist government. Conservative party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo plans to participate in the demonstration in Madrid, in addition to a trip to Ceuta, and instructed all regional associations to do the same in their regions. The gesture costs nothing. However, in other regions of Spain, there is skepticism about what would truly help Ceuta – a distribution of the remaining refugees across the country.

image.author: Epa
image.caption: Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the Conservatives.
image.altText: Alberto Núñez Feijóo leader of the Partido Popular

content.caption: Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the Conservatives.
content.author: Epa

content.text: A month after the influx, such a step in overcrowded Ceuta continues to fail due to the registration of migrants. On Friday, Spain requested support from the EU border agency Frontex and Europol for the triage of refugees and the processing of their applications. Brussels had already offered such assistance on several previous occasions, first at the end of July.

Government sources now privately admit that the extent of the crisis was underestimated even after its outbreak. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has often proved to be an adept manager in the past, but in the Ceuta case, even allies do not give him high marks. Sánchez visited Ceuta on July 31 but has not returned to a city that, at times, the whole world was watching.

On Monday morning, he attempted to regain interpretive authority through a ninety-minute radio interview. During his vacation, his cabinet had not projected a favorable image. Key ministers Fernando Grande-Marlaska (Interior) and Margarita Robles (Defense) presented contradictory versions of the extent to which the intelligence service had been informed about the impending influx before July 30. Sánchez attempted to mediate on Monday, stating there had been information, but none about the extent. Russian and Israeli cyberactivists were responsible for this, he claimed, as they had spread the false news of an open border after the first arrivals. Both countries denied this involvement.

Under the vague hope for Europe, up to 80,000 people arrived in the city, which barely has more inhabitants, at the end of July. Days later, the government spoke of 72,000 people, stating that only about 2,000 remained in the city. This was intended to emphasize how quickly and smoothly a large proportion of the migrants had been repatriated.

image.author: Marcos Moreno / Getty
image.caption: People sleep outside reception centers to be the first in line for newly available places. Spain's government has announced plans to gradually increase capacity to 6,000 beds.
image.altText: CEUTA, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 01: Dozens of migrants continue to sleep in the vicinity of Loma Colmenar, as of September 1, 2026, in Ceuta, Spain. Dozens of people spent the night in the vicinity of Loma Colmenar, despite the intervention of the National Police after hundreds of Maghreb migrants attempted to enter the city en masse. The situation necessitated the deployment of a large police force, which carried out charges to contain the crowd and fired warning shots into the air in an attempt to bring the situation under control. (Photo By Marcos Moreno/Europa Press via Getty Images)

content.caption: People sleep outside reception centers to be the first in line for newly available places. Spain's government has announced plans to gradually increase capacity to 6,000 beds.
content.author: Marcos Moreno / Getty

content.text: However, the numbers were clearly too optimistic. A larger number of minors and potentially asylum seekers were among the arrivals. Neither group may be expelled through an expedited procedure. The government had raised false hopes, a fatal political error. On Thursday, Sánchez will justify himself before Congress.

Meanwhile, Madrid speaks of 5,000 remaining refugees, while other sources cite a figure of 8,000 people. On Monday, distribution struggles broke out among migrants outside the reception centers over newly provided sleeping places. Police had to intervene with warning shots. Sánchez stated that 3,300 beds were currently available, with a target of 6,000. On Tuesday, the cabinet approved a new aid package of 168 million euros for Ceuta, which is expected to grow to 309 million by the end of the year.

The relationship with Morocco also remains a point of contention. The opposition criticizes the government's unwavering praise of cooperation with the neighboring state and its exoneration from responsibility for the border storm. Sánchez, for his part, announced his intention to arrange a visit by the King to Ceuta. Conservative governments had never dared to do this in the past. Morocco claims the exclave, and a visit by the Spanish head of state is considered a maximum provocation. Sánchez's announcement is apparently intended to show, against this backdrop, that someone like him is the last to lose courage.

playableVideoTeasers.title: NZZ Format | Europe's new cocaine front – how drug gangs are infiltrating Spain's coastal towns
playableVideoTeasers.description: For years, cocaine use has been rising in Europe, generating lucrative business for criminal gangs. Now, southern Spain is becoming an increasingly important hub for smugglers. For the people in the tranquil coastal towns, this has sometimes had dramatic consequences. Many tourists appreciate Andalusia for its stunning beaches, idyllic villages, and cozy tapas bars. But Europe's southernmost region also has another face: Here, criminal gangs are expanding, supplying all of Europe with cocaine. «We have a veritable drug economy here,» says social worker Alma Jugado. Andalusia is one of the poorest regions in Spain. Drug smugglers here earn more in a single night than others do in a month. So-called TikTok narcos—influencers who portray the smuggler's life as a big party—contribute to the popularity of the illegal trade. Law enforcement is forced to conduct increasingly dangerous operations while simultaneously becoming increasingly powerless. The documentary delves deep into Andalusia's smuggling business. She accompanies customs officers, social workers – and an investigative journalist who wants to meet with one of the masterminds behind the drug gangs. It becomes clear that the rising crime in southern Spain is far more than a local problem.
